title: Cardiac Arrest and the Chain of Survival

scenes.narration: Module one: cardiac arrest and the Chain of Survival. This is the heart, beating about seventy times a minute. Each beat begins as an electrical impulse that spreads through the muscle, so the atria and then the ventricles contract in sequence, pushing blood into the aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Cardiac arrest is what happens when that electrical coordination fails.
scenes.title: Cardiac Arrest and the Chain of Survival

scenes.narration: In ventricular fibrillation, thousands of muscle fibres fire out of step. The ventricles stop contracting as one; they quiver. A quivering ventricle ejects no blood, so cardiac output falls to zero, and within seconds the pulse is gone. The brain receives no oxygen: the patient becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally, sometimes with occasional gasps. This is a heart that has failed electrically, not a heart starved of blood, and that difference decides what you do next.

notes.note: Ventricular fibrillation: the fibres fire out of step
Cardiac arrest: an electrical failure of the pump

scenes.narration: These two are often confused. In a heart attack, a coronary artery is blocked and part of the heart muscle is starved of blood, but the heart usually keeps beating: the patient is typically awake, often with chest pain. In cardiac arrest the problem is electrical, the heart stops pumping, and the patient is unresponsive with no pulse. A heart attack can trigger cardiac arrest, but only arrest needs compressions now.
rows: Circulation: a coronary artery is blocked
Unresponsive, no normal breathing, no pulse
Usually awake, often with chest pain

scenes.narration: Cardiac arrest has four possible rhythms, and the rhythm on the monitor decides the treatment. Two are shockable: ventricular fibrillation, and pulseless ventricular tachycardia, where the ventricles beat so fast they cannot fill. A shock depolarises the whole muscle at once, giving the heart's own pacemaker a chance to take over, and compressions continue around it. The other two are not shockable: pulseless electrical activity, with electrical activity but no pulse, and asystole, with no electrical activity at all. Here a shock cannot help, so compressions continue while the team searches for a reversible cause.

flowchart LR

scenes.narration: How often do patients survive? Outside hospital, about 350,000 people a year in the United States have a cardiac arrest, and nine in ten of them die. Overall survival to discharge is about 10.5%. It is 21.1% in a public place, where someone is more likely to see the collapse and act, but only 8.9% at home. In hospital, survival is higher, 23.6% for adults and 45.2% for children, because the arrest is usually witnessed and help is close. Yet only about 41% of people receive compressions from a bystander before help arrives.

notes.note: About 350,000 out-of-hospital arrests a year in the United States
Only about 41% receive bystander compressions before help arrives

scenes.narration: That is why the nearest person matters most. Without circulation the brain begins to suffer within minutes, and every minute without compressions or a shock lowers the chance of survival. Chest compressions squeeze the heart between the sternum and the spine, pushing blood to the brain and to the heart muscle itself. Started immediately, compressions can double or even triple survival. In the first three minutes, the actions of the nearest person matter more than everything that follows.

notes.note: Every minute without compressions lowers survival
Immediate compressions can double or triple survival
The first three minutes belong to the nearest person

scenes.narration: The 2025 guidelines describe survival as one Chain of Survival, for adults and children, in hospital and outside it. Its six links run in order. Early recognition and activation: someone recognises the arrest and calls for help. High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation: compressions, and breaths, especially for children and in opioid-related arrest. Defibrillation, as early as possible. Advanced resuscitation by the code team. Post-cardiac arrest care. And recovery and survivorship. Each link depends on the one before it.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
 A[Recognition and activation]:::red --> B[High-quality CPR] --> C[Defibrillation] --> D[Advanced resuscitation] --> E[Post-arrest care] --> F[Recovery and survivorship]:::teal

scenes.narration: If you trained on the 2020 guidelines, you are updating, not relearning. Four separate chains became one. The terms changed: rescue breaths are now simply breaths, and ventilation now means mechanical support. The compression rate stays at 100 to 120 a minute, and single-rescuer adult resuscitation stays at 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

To summarise. Cardiac arrest is an electrical failure that stops the heart's output. Two of its four rhythms can be shocked. And survival depends on six links, the first of which is you. In the next module, you will learn to recognise deterioration and arrest, and how to call for help.

notes.note: Cardiac arrest: an electrical failure that stops output
Shockable: VF and pulseless VT · not shockable: PEA and asystole
